title: From Memory to Palm Leaves
bigQuestion: How did the Buddha's teachings travel from spoken words to the books we have today?

story.title: Five Hundred in a Cave
story.kicker: Five hundred monks sit in a cave, and one of them begins, "Thus have I heard."
paragraphs: Buddhist tradition tells this story. A few months after the Buddha died, his students gathered near the city of Rajagaha. They met in a large cave in the hills. Five hundred senior monks came.
They had a big worry. The Buddha had taught for many years. But he had written nothing down. How would they keep his words safe? Some of the monks looked at one another in silence.
First a monk named Upali stood. He recited the rules for monks and nuns. The others listened closely. When he finished, they agreed that his words were correct.
Then Ananda stood. He had been the Buddha's helper for many years. He had heard more teachings than anyone. The cave was quiet. Ananda began: "Thus have I heard."
The monks chanted the teachings back together. Buddhists call this meeting the First Council. For hundreds of years after, the teachings lived in memory and chanting.
story.think: Why might a group chanting together help keep words from changing?

lessons.title: The First Council
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says the Buddha's students met after his death to recite and agree on his teachings.
reading: Buddhist tradition says a meeting was held soon after the Buddha died. It is called the First *Council*. A council is a meeting to decide something important. Tradition places it at Rajagaha, in northern India.
The Vinaya tells the story. It says 500 monks attended. Upali recited the rules. Ananda recited the talks. The group agreed on what they heard. Then they chanted it together.
Scholars cannot check every detail of this story. Many think the texts grew and changed over time. Buddhists and scholars both agree the teachings were first passed on by voice, not writing.

words.d: a meeting to decide something important
to say something aloud from memory

lessons.title: Ananda's Memory
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition remembers Ananda as the monk with the best memory, who recited the suttas.
reading: *Ananda* was the Buddha's cousin. For about 25 years he was the Buddha's personal helper. He walked beside him and brought him water. He heard many talks.
Buddhists remember Ananda for his memory. Tradition says he could repeat a teaching after hearing it once. That is why the council asked him to recite.
Ananda is also remembered for his kindness. The Vinaya says he spoke up for women who wanted to become nuns. Many Buddhists honor him for that today. Nuns still tell this story.

words.d: the Buddha's cousin and helper, remembered for his memory
the ability to keep and recall what you learned

look.title: A Helper Who Listened
look.text: Picture a monk walking one step behind his teacher every day for years. He carries a water pot. He listens to every talk. At night he repeats the words to himself.
look.prompt: Why would a helper like this be good at remembering?

check.q: How was Ananda related to the Buddha?
check.why: Tradition says Ananda was the Buddha's cousin.

check.q: What is Ananda remembered for?

check.q: Who did Ananda speak up for, says the Vinaya?

check.why: The Vinaya says Ananda asked the Buddha to let women become nuns.

lessons.title: Chanting Together
lessons.mainIdea: For centuries, monks kept the teachings by chanting them together.
reading: After the council, groups of monks memorized different parts of the texts. They chanted them together, again and again. This is called oral *tradition*.
Chanting together helps catch mistakes. If one monk says a word wrong, the others notice. Repeated lists and phrases made the texts easier to remember.
Scholars say the suttas show signs of this. They repeat whole lines many times. They use numbered lists, like the Four Noble Truths. These help memory.

words.d: teachings passed on by speaking and memory, not writing
to say or sing words together in a steady rhythm

look.title: Why Repeat?
look.text: A song has a chorus that comes back again and again. Soon you know it by heart. The suttas often repeat whole lines, too. A student hears the pattern and remembers.
look.prompt: What songs or rhymes do you know by heart? Why do you remember them?

check.q: What is oral tradition?
choices: passing on teachings by speaking and memory
check.why: Oral tradition passes teachings on by voice and memory.

check.q: How does chanting together help?
check.why: When a group chants, a wrong word gets noticed.

check.q: What helped monks remember the suttas?
check.why: Scholars point to repetition and lists as memory aids.

lessons.title: Palm Leaves in Sri Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition records that the Pali Canon was first written down on palm leaves in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE.
reading: Buddhism reached Sri Lanka around the 3rd century BCE. Monks there kept chanting the texts. Then came hard times, with war and famine. Many monks died.
The Sri Lankan chronicles say monks worried the teachings might be lost. So they wrote them down. Tradition places this at Aluvihara in the 1st century BCE.
They wrote on *palm leaves*. Writers scratched letters into dried leaves with a metal pen. Then they rubbed in ink or soot to make the letters dark. The leaves were tied into bundles.

words.d: a dried leaf used as a page for writing in South and Southeast Asia
a history book that lists events in order

lessons.title: Making a Palm-Leaf Book
lessons.mainIdea: Palm-leaf books were made by hand, and copies had to be made again and again.
reading: A palm-leaf book is long and thin. Each leaf has holes. A string runs through the holes. Wooden covers protect the pages. The covers are often painted or carved with care.
Palm leaves slowly wear out. Heat, bugs and damp harm them. So monks copied the texts onto new leaves every so often. Copying was careful, slow work. A copy could take months.
Many Buddhist temples in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar still keep palm-leaf books. Some libraries study them today. Very old leaves are rare, because most wore out.

words.d: to write something again so there is another one

look.title: Holding a Palm-Leaf Book
look.text: Picture a bundle of long, narrow leaves, as wide as your hand. Tiny dark letters run across them. Two wooden boards hold the bundle. A string ties it closed.
look.prompt: What problems might a palm-leaf book have in a hot, wet place?

check.q: What is a manuscript?
check.why: A manuscript is a handwritten book.

check.q: Why did monks copy palm-leaf books?

check.q: What holds a palm-leaf book together?
check.why: A string runs through holes in the leaves.

lessons.title: The Diamond Sutra of 868
lessons.mainIdea: A printed Diamond Sutra from 868 CE is the oldest dated printed book known.
reading: In 1900 a monk in Dunhuang, China, found a hidden cave room. It was full of old scrolls. One was a copy of the *Diamond Sutra*, a Mahayana text. The cave had been sealed for centuries.
It was printed with carved wooden blocks. At the end it gives a date that matches 868 CE. It says a man named Wang Jie had it made for his parents. It is the oldest dated printed book known.
Today it is kept at the British Library in London. The scroll is about 16 feet long. It shows how Buddhists in China used printing to share their texts.

words.d: a Mahayana sutra; a printed copy from 868 CE is the oldest dated printed book known
printing by pressing carved wooden blocks with ink onto paper

lessons.title: Into Chinese and Tibetan
lessons.mainIdea: Translators carried Buddhist texts into Chinese and Tibetan over many centuries.
reading: Buddhism reached China by about the 1st century CE. Translators worked for centuries to turn texts into Chinese. One famous translator was Kumarajiva, around 400 CE.
Buddhism reached Tibet in the 7th and 8th centuries CE. Tibetan scholars made careful *translations* from Sanskrit. They made word lists so each term was translated the same way.
Some texts now survive only in Chinese or Tibetan. Without these translators, many sutras would be lost. Buddhists in East Asia and Tibet read them in their own languages.

words.d: a text turned from one language into another
a person who turns words from one language into another

look.title: One Word, Many Languages
look.text: The Sanskrit word for the teaching is dharma. In Pali it is dhamma. In Chinese it is fa. In Tibetan it is cho. It is one idea carried in many words.
look.prompt: Why is translating a sacred word so hard?

check.q: Who was Kumarajiva?
check.why: Kumarajiva translated many sutras into Chinese around 400 CE.

check.q: What did Tibetan scholars make to help translate?
check.why: They made word lists so each term was translated the same way.

check.q: What is the Pali form of dharma?
check.why: Dharma is Sanskrit and dhamma is Pali.

lessons.title: Into English
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars began translating Buddhist texts into English in the 1800s, and Chicago hosted Buddhist speakers in 1893.
reading: In the 1800s, European scholars began to study Pali and Sanskrit. F. Max Muller translated the Dhammapada in 1881. T.W. Rhys Davids translated suttas that same year. He also founded the Pali Text Society in 1881.
In 1893 the World's *Parliament* of Religions met in Chicago. Two Buddhist speakers came. Anagarika Dharmapala came from Sri Lanka. Soyen Shaku, a Zen teacher, came from Japan.
Today many translations exist. Buddhist monks, nuns and scholars all translate. Some translations are free online. Readers can compare them side by side.

words.d: a large meeting of religious leaders held in Chicago in 1893
a group founded in 1881 to publish Pali texts and translations
